descriptionChirho: To physically turn one's body, changing the direction one faces. Used of Jesus or others turning around in narrative contexts: Mark 5:30 (Jesus turned in the crowd sensing the woman's touch), Mark 8:33 (Jesus turned and rebuked Peter), John 21:20 (Peter turned and saw the beloved disciple), Acts 9:40 (Peter turned to the body of Tabitha), Acts 16:18 (Paul turned to address the spirit), Rev 1:12 (John turned to see the voice speaking). Cross-linguistically: Arabic iltafata (turned around), Hebrew panah (turned/faced), Hindi mudkar (having turned), Korean dolaseoseo/dorikeyeo (turning around), Spanish volviendose/habiendose vuelto (having turned), French se-tourner. The physical motion is concrete and spatial, distinguishing this from the metaphorical spiritual senses.

To go back or come back to a previous location or starting point, denoting spatial return without spiritual connotation. Used of peace returning to a house (Matt 10:13), a demon returning to its dwelling (Matt 12:44), Jesus's command not to turn back for possessions (Matt 24:18, Mark 13:16, Luke 17:31), the shepherds returning to their flocks (Luke 2:39), the girl's spirit returning to her body (Luke 8:55), Luke 17:4 (returning in repentance but with physical 'coming back'), Barnabas and Paul returning to visit churches (Acts 15:36), Peter returning to the shepherd (1 Pet 2:25), the dog returning to its vomit (2 Pet 2:22). Cross-linguistically: Arabic rajaa (returned), Hebrew shuv/khazar (return), Hindi lautkar/lautna (return), Korean doragada (go back), Spanish volver (return), French retourner/se-tourner.

To turn back to God or turn away from sin in a moral or spiritual conversion, often synonymous with metanoia (repentance). Used in Isaiah quotations about hardened hearts not turning (Matt 13:15, Mark 4:12, Acts 28:27), Peter's call to repentance (Acts 3:19), Paul's mission to turn Gentiles from idols (Acts 14:15, 15:19, 26:18,20), the veil removed when one turns to the Lord (2 Cor 3:16), the Galatians turning back to weak elements (Gal 4:9), the Thessalonians who turned to God from idols (1 Thess 1:9). Cross-linguistically: Arabic yarjiuu (turn back to God), Hebrew yashuvu (they shall return/repent), Hindi phirna (turn), Korean dorikida (turn/convert), Spanish convertirse/volverse (convert/turn). The spiritual dimension is signaled by the theological context and confirmed by translation choices like Spanish convertir rather than mere volver.

To turn or redirect someone else, causing them to return or convert; the transitive-causative use of epistrepho. In Luke 1:16-17 the angel prophesies that John the Baptist will turn (epistrephsei) many of the sons of Israel to the Lord, and will turn (epistrepsai) the hearts of fathers to children. In Acts 26:18 Paul's mission is to turn people from darkness to light. In James 5:19-20 whoever turns back (epistrephse/epistrepsas) a sinner from error saves a soul from death. Cross-linguistically: Arabic yaruddu/liyadruda (cause to return), Hebrew yashiv/lehashiv (causative hiphil of shuv, cause to return), Hindi pherna (cause to turn), Korean dorikige hada (make someone turn), Spanish hacer volver/convertir (make return/convert). The Hebrew hiphil form lehashiv in Luke 1:16-17 confirms the causative reading, distinguishing this from the intransitive senses.
